PROPOSED REVIEW OF PROVISION WHICH PREVENTS
subsubtopic: DISCLOSURE OF GROUNDS FOR FIRING PERSON AS SECURITY RISK-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Superior Court Chief Justice Jules Des-chenes recently ruled that the RCMP does not have to reveal the reasons which lead to the firing of two young Montreal women from their Olympic jobs on the ground of national security and on the recommendation of the RCMP. The Chief Justice based this ruling upon a 1970 amendment to the law of the federal court which sanctioned in five specific cases the principle of absolute executive immunity, but he pointed out that a different rule prevailed in the United States, England, Australia and New Zealand.
Inasmuch as this Canadian rule is inconsistent with the Canadian Bill of Rights, which entitles any person to a fair hearing, and in view of the importance of secrecy of official documents being confined to a minimum I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Solicitor General be instructed to review the law in this regard and introduce legislation which would change the principle of absolute executive immunity in such cases to one of relative immunity, subject to review by the courts.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF STUDIES MADE ON DISTRIBUTION OF FISCAL INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance.
Even though the right hon. Prime Minister answered me recently that it was too theoretical an approach to make an evaluation of the funds collected and spent by the federal government in every province, would the minister tell the House whether he has nevertheless undertaken such a study within his department so that all Canadians, particularly Quebecers, could know for sure how tax revenues are shared in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF STUDIES MADE ON DISTRIBUTION OF FISCAL INCOME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have already had the opportunity to answer such a question. I said it was possible, with tax figures, to make such an evaluation for the whole country and for each province. But in a broader sense, the benefits derived from Confederation involve some rather arbitrary judgments on the sharing of government's expenses and goods between the various provinces of Canada and in that sense such an evaluation has necessarily to be interpreted as arbitrary. However, I can confirm that with the tax statistics produced by Statistics Canada, we have figures which can be prepared to meet these needs.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to announce today a federal government initiative for the young people of our country in the form of a year-round travel exchange program developed in the Department of the Secretary of State. The program will be based on the principle of twinning and, when fully operational, will involve between 20,000 and 30,000 young people per year.
Hon. members will recall that in the last Speech from the Throne on October 12, 1976, the government committed itself to federal initiatives designed specifically for youth. My department's new travel exchange program, to be known as "Open House Canada/Hospitalite Canada", is one component of these initiatives. Information on other projects will be available within the coming month. Our new program will enable young people, both individually and in groups, to participate in exchange visits with others across the country. In taking this initiative, the government is responding directly to the young people of Canada. We have all seen examples of youth taking such initiatives on their own, assuming the burden of the cost of these initiatives, and in so doing demon-
March 24, 1977

strating to the rest of us how much they care about their country and that they would like to get to know it better.
I am also aware of the valuable contributions made for many years in the area of youth exchanges by voluntary organizations. It is our intention to continue to work closely with them to achieve our common goals.
[ Translation]
I have also noted a kind of tacit agreement in the press and in the House to the effect that some people would like us to promote further visits and exchanges among Canadians. The Commissioner of Official Languages has often complained about the fact that many Canadians know the United States and Europe better than some parts of their own country, especially the areas where another language is spoken.
"Open House Canada/Hospitalite Canada" is designed for the generation that will produce our leaders in the decades to come. Those participating as individuals will be from 16 to 22 years of age and those participating in groups will be from 14 to 22 years of age. Their transportation costs will be paid by the federal government but each traveller will be expected to pay a small participation fee.
The mechanics of the program, although not yet worked out in fine detail, will proceed along the following lines: young Canadians interested in participating will apply to a central bureau where they will be matched with an individual or group from another province. Once the twinning is established, the participants will be encouraged to have exploratory correspondence and other types of exchanges with each other in order to establish rapport and then eventually to visit each other in their homes. Further details will be available in a month, and application forms for those who wish to participate will be ready in June.

While we put the emphasis on mutual exchanges among participants, the program does provide allowances for individuals or groups who would take part only as visitors or as hosts. [English]
The aim of the program, then, is to create an encouraging environment for what we look upon as an extremely desirable national purpose: the year around discovery of Canada by the young people of our country. By removing the cost barriers involved in travel, we feel we shall not only be encouraging, but also challenging young Canadians to do something for the unity of their country.

Through that program we hope to encourage a dialogue and a closer understanding among Canadians, especially among those who speak English or French, as well as between the regions and provinces giving an opportunity to the young people to get acquainted with a new style of living and environment.
Open House Canada

In concluding, may I say that I am convinced Canada's reputation around the world for openness and hospitality is deserved. We are now offering an opportunity for Canadians to be open and hospitable to each other.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
I am also very glad that the statement has come within a day or two of a rather extraordinary statement about a bilingual program which affected only two of the ten provinces and two territories-a program of Ontario-Quebec travel. Obviously, the minister has recognized, a day or two late, that there is more to Canada than his province of Ontario or the great province of Quebec. I am glad this program has been redressed.
A few years ago there was an anguished cry in the United States-"What have they done to our children?" It was made in times of frustration in American national life. I am anxious that such an anguished cry will never be heard in this country, because we will have done something for our young people. Unhappily, though, the rather interesting initiatives and travel plans are not matched-and I mean this as a positive criticism-with initiatives by the Department of Manpower and Immigration for the 350,000 Canadians under 25 years of age who have nothing to do, who are out of work. What I am really saying is that if the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) has an initiative for the young, the Department of Manpower and Immigration must gear up and pay particular attention to Canadians under 25 years of age who are seeking work.
This particular week is a rather opportune time for the minister to make his statement. The galleries are often filled, because of school breaks in various provinces and because of a rather imaginative program run by a volunteer organization which brings young people from the high schools of Canada into the capital. I do not want to be preachy or self-righteous, but I think the fact that we have visitors this week, and the fact that the minister has said there will be other visitors all

March 24, 1977
Open House Canada
through the year puts a special onus on us as members of parliament. In a way, we are on exhibit here: the way we respond, our sensitivities, and so on, will be marked and carefully analysed, I hope, by those who do us the honour of sitting in the galleries this week and in years to come.
The young Canadians who are travelling may well be our sons and daughters. They will not be mine, because mine have travelled and are now young men and women. I cannot help but say that I hope, as we extend hospitality, we will not shut doors to people because their costumes may not be the same as we would travel in, or their hair might be a different length. In other words, if young people travelling wear jeans and have a pack on their backs, the hospitality program should be aware that this is the dress and mode of the young today.
I have never got over the fact that somebody told me once that when they saw someone on the road hitchhiking who wore blue jeans, they called the RCMP. My horrified response was that the person in jeans who was hitchhiking might be my son or daughter. I know the minister wants to think that in a hospitality program we welcome the young in their various modes of dress and with their various concerns, which I very much hope will not be identical to those of us who are part of this "splendid" status quo.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to thank the minister for sending an advance copy of the statement. We in the New Democratic Party welcome this initiative by the minister to assist young people in exchanging visits in all parts of the country. I think we should have had more of this in the past than has been our experience.
I think, too, that with the high rate of unemployment among young people-about double the national rate-a lot of young people will have plenty of time on their hands this summer to take advantage of the program. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) noted, it is unfortunate that we can find initiatives in the Department of the Secretary of State to meet the needs of young people but cannot find the same degree of commitment in the Department of Manpower and Immigration. I think the federal initiative should be looked at carefully by all the provinces, and I hope we will see some initiatives at the provincial level as well in terms of exchanges between the regions of Canada.
The minister's statement is not precise in some details, and I should like to raise some questions. I am concerned about the selection process, and just who will be chosen. I should like to make sure there is a built-in mechanism to guarantee as broad a representation as possible. Not only should we have people participating from large and small urban centres, but they should be from the rural areas as well. There should also be some guarantee that it will not be just one particular income group that will receive the benefit. I hope there will be some form of proportional representation in that regard.

I hope that one of the conditions of eligibility will be a guarantee by the young people involved that they will take part in follow-up programs, so to speak, after their visits are over. In this way they could share their experiences and knowledge. Perhaps they could report to fellow students in schools, seek out the local media in their communities and ask them to report and appear before service clubs and other interested groups.
In conclusion, I welcome the initiative. We want to know more of the details. Let me echo the sentiments of the late Governor General, Georges Vanier who in his 1967 New Year's message said that one of the strengths of this country was its diversity; that we should open the doors and windows of the provinces so that we could see one another, meet one another, share our experiences and so promote understanding and unity. I hope this program will in some small way fulfil the wish of our late and distinguished Governor General, Georges Vanier.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the Secretary of State is launching a program of a permanent nature through which young Canadians of 14 to 22 are being invited, individually or in groups, to take part in exchange visits throughout Canada. It will be remembered that a similar program of exchanges already exists between Quebec and Ontario. I am of course very happy with the praiseworthy initiative of extending the program throughout Canada. I feel that it is even desirable. As a youth, I myself was able to take part in a similar program, though its purposes were different. The young people in eastern Canada were encouraged to go and help bring in the crops out west; all they had to reimburse was $10 for their travelling expenses.
We were paid to harvest the crops. Of course we were working but for myself and the other young people of my age it was a very enriching experience. It is essential for each young Canadian to get a better knowledge of his country and of the desires, the problems and the views of others in all provinces. We never know enough about our own country. So I wish to thank the minister for having given such importance to the commitment made in the last Speech from the Throne last October 12. However, I have some reservations based on our experience with similar programs. An excellent program is often smothered and thwarted by a heavy, slow and inefficient bureaucracy which ignores the wishes clearly expressed by the citizen, young or not so young, who wants to benefit from a government program.
As usual, hon. members are informed of the major aspects of a government project which seems excellent in principle, but what will happen in practice? Civil servants are the only ones who know, for instance the members of the future secretariate announced today by the minister. The population must realize the fact that when members of parliament vote for a program generally proposed by a minister, they do not vote on rules, requirements or selection criteria. The whole implementation
Marth 24, 1977

of a program is the sole responsibility of bureaucracy. Members of parliament have nothing to say on that matter.
This is why we can say today that the intention seems excellent. The objective is supported by every member of the Social Credit Party. Our party believes that Canada should be better understood and we must encourage any program that will allow our fellow citizens, particularly young Canadians, to gain a better insight of the real dimensions of their country. In doing this we might have fewer extremists on one side or the other or in one province or the other. Through a better knowledge of Canada by future generations, politicians in general might stop trying to benefit from divisions among us in Canada, owing to the vigilance of those future Canadian adults.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext: Order please. The rules with respect to ministerial statements under which we operate give the Chair a great deal of discretion with respect to questions following a statement. It is apparent that the minister's statement, the details of which are to follow later, has aroused no disagreement. Hon. members, obviously, do not disagree with it. Therefore, I do not propose to allow a great deal of questioning. However, I note that the hon. members for Lanark-Ren-frew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), for Battle River (Mr. Malone), for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury), and for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) are interested in putting questions. I ask them to be brief.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall ask my questions slowly in order to allow the minister to make notes. He indicated that the applications will be ready in June. Is it intended, after these applications have been processed, to let the exchanges take place in July and August this year when students will be out of school and our youth unemployment is the highest in our history. For how long will the exchange students be away? Will their visits last a week, two weeks, one month, or perhaps even two months? Could the minister be more specific? Also, can he say how many young people he hopes will be involved. He is under a budgetary limitation, I am sure-I do not know if it is $1,000, $3,000 or even $10,000 per student. Does the minister at present expect the program to continue each year, say for the next five years, or will it be in place only this year and perhaps next year?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can reply briefly to the perceptive questions of the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). I mentioned June as the month when applications will be available, and we hope strongly that the exchange will begin in the summer, in July and August. Perhaps the initial exchanges will involve groups rather than individuals because of the longer lead time we may need to establish procedures for the placing of individuals who may wish to make visits back and forth from one part of the country to another.
To answer the hon. member's second question, the program is designed to support travel costs. Its purpose is not to assist tourism-let me put it that way. It is designed to establish an
Open House Canada
exchange of views and contacts between individuals in different parts of the country. We shall be considering some requirement for a minimum length of stay which could be perhaps a week. If individuals wish to stay longer-for two or three weeks or one month-that would not affect the travel cost portion of the government's participation. The travel costs will remain the same, no matter how long people stay. There would need to be a minimum time requirement, but the length of the visit can be extended for a considerable period since that would not affect the cost of the government's participation.
I cannot say how many people will be involved in the program. We shall be able to assess numbers in the light of demand, But we believe, initially, that when the program becomes fully operational it will involve between 20,000 and
30.000	young people a year.
It is intended to continue the program indefinitely although, of course, in light of our experience we may refine, alter or change it. Experience may indicate some better ways of meeting our objectives. In initial terms, we are not thinking so much of a dollar figure as of the participation of between
20.000	and 30,000 young people between the ages of 14 and
22.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the return of the spirit of centennial year in the form of some of the programs initiated for that year-after an unfortunate lapse. Can the minister tell us if other programs of this kind will be announced in time for older people to be involved in interprovincial exchanges this summer? Too many good things in life have been reserved for the young. Under the former exchange programs there were opportunities for adult groups and families to get to know their fellow Canadians in other provinces. I wonder if there soon will be an announcement to extend the scope of this program to people other than the young, even though I think the minister has started in the right place.
In addition to organized programs, is the minister considering, as well, less structured schemes whereby families can travel the country? Particularly at a time when we are trying to encourage rail traffic, perhaps once a year each family in Canada might have the privilege of travelling to another province by rail at no cost. It would simply reduce the subsidies that this government will have to pay to the new Via Rail system. Why not a Via Rail visa for every family in Canada?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) applauding. He, obviously, would like to take advantage of extending the program to those other than the young. He is youthful in spirit but would not, under the present age limits of this program, be eligible for a twinning arrangement. The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) really anticipated in his second question my response to his first. The orientation of this program is specifically, as I indicated, for young people be-

March 24, 1977
Open House Canada
tween the ages of 14 and 22 or 16 and 22 on individual exchanges.
We did consider the possibilities of finding some means of assisting with the transportation costs of young people and their families, or within the context of their families, in an exchange or twinning arrangement. That is, indeed, an intriguing and interesting idea. We felt that at the present time there were certain administrative difficulties to such a plan. We felt we could not wait until we had ironed out all those difficulties before proceeding with the steps I described in the House today. This is a matter upon which we will continue to reflect.
Without in any way making a commitment, I would say that this is a subject we will consider, in light of our experience with the program, to see whether some extension toward families may be contemplated some time later, probably in subsequent years rather than this year.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to congratulate the minister on initiating this program. I want to ask two brief questions. The first is whether this will be a continuing program. We had an excellent exchange program. I know that groups of high school students from my province visited the province of Quebec, and students from the province of Quebec came to stay in the homes and visit the communities from which I come. There has been an ongoing correspondence ever since, which is of great benefit. Unfortunately, the program was stopped. Is this likely to be an ongoing program, or a one-shot deal? Second, will groups, particularly groups of students who make application, be able to arrange exchange programs so that the young people they visit will make reciprocal visits in order to see each other in their home territory?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to both questions is "yes". The program is envisaged as a continuing one. It is not intended that it should expire after one year, or be, as the hon. member terms it, a one-shot program. We are looking at a continuing program of government. Yes, indeed, groups of students will be eligible. The essence of the program is to adopt the idea the hon. member expressed in his question, that is to say, there should be an exchange.
One's ability to take advantage of the program and visit a student, or a particular group of students to visit another group of students, will depend upon willingness to accept, in return, a visit from that individual or group. There may be a few exceptions to that principle in the application of the program. There may be some people who will be hosts and who will not feel they are able to go on a subsequent visit. But the general theme of the program will be on the basis of twinning; that is to say, that people will be accepted as eligible under the program to visit another part of the country if they will in turn accept a reciprocal visit.
While I am on my feet, I should indicate to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) that I welcome his support. Indeed, I welcome the support indicated by all parties in the House. This is not a partisan or party measure. It is one which responds to the wishes of all parties and all members of

the House. I welcome the support for the program. I hope hon. members will do what they can to make the program effective and tell young people about it.
I should say that the concerns which the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie raised about how people will be chosen, and whether this will be a program which will meet only the needs of a narrow segment of the population, are concerns we had. We are determined to ensure that it covers a broad range of social and economic status, geographical representation, and so on. There should be a continual method of follow-up.
It is not, as I said earlier, a tourism program. It is designed to share human contact, exchange and understanding on a continuing basis.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to pay tribute to the minister for introducing this legislation. I find it noteworthy for a country as diverse as Canada. While I very much appreciate the spirit of what the minister is attempting to do, there is a bit of conflict in relation to something that is already going on. The minister mentioned the value of the cultural exchange, something none of us would deny. However, at the present time there is an international exchange going on in Alberta, particularly with Scandinavian families and their host families back home. It has been going on for about a decade. I would point out that an airplane of Scandinavian people landing in this country at the international airport in Edmonton were unable to get off the airplane because the federal government had not completed its paperwork. About a year ago they were about to get on an airplane in a Scandinavian country-I believe in Oslo- but the paperwork was not done.
In talking to the people who have been putting these exchanges together, each successive one has been a series of continuing roadblocks. I will supply the minister with further information because I know he needs greater detail with regard to this. First, will the minister review the whole matter of this international exchange of people going to work in other countries? Second, will he bypass the representation he is getting directly, and talk to the families who have been hosting these exchanges for a long period of time about the value they think the program has, so that he can have direct input and representation from them on what they consider to be an extremely important international exchange?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF STUDENT TRAVEL EXCHANGE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for raising the point. I will await the information which he is sending to me. I am not aware, specifically, of the program he has mentioned, nor am I aware of the difficulties which have been encountered in relation to it. From his description, I am not sure whether those difficulties really relate to my jurisdiction. They may relate to external affairs or immigration. When the hon. member sends me details of the problem which these families have faced, I will ensure they are brought to the attention of the proper minister to be looked into and, I hope, settled.
I must say, with frankness, to the hon. member that the purpose of this exchange is not set within the international
March 24, 1977

context. It is to encourage young Canadians to get to know one another better and to get to know parts of Canada better. I have often been disturbed to find that Canadians know other countries better than their own. For example, people in my city of Toronto often find it easier to take holidays in Florida, or Europe, than to take holidays in Canada in areas such as that represented by the hon. member. A way should be found to get them to know one another as well, and to know other parts of the country.

speechtext:
1.	With reference to the answer to Question No. 1,605, does the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources promote the concept that temperature comfort levels depend on a combination of the heat levels and humidity levels?
2.	Does the Minister believe that economies can be affected in winter by increasing humidity levels with corresponding reductions in the setting of the thermostat?
3.	Does the Department intend to promote the use of dehumidification systems in summer as a means of reducing the consumption of fuel for air cooling purposes?
[Mr. Wenman.J

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: TEMPERATURE COMFORT LEVELS
speechtext:
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources reports as follows: 1. The effectiveness of humidity in allowing lower temperature settings is uncertain. The equipment guide (1972) of the American society of heating refrigeration and air conditioning engineers states the following: Human Comfort. The effect of relative humidity on all aspects of human comfort has not as yet been completely established. From the standpoint of thermal comfort, it has usually been assumed that higher temperatures are required to offset the effect of decreased relative humidity. This is exemplified by the effective temperature lines of the basic ASHRAE Comfort Chart, which was developed through studies of the immediate reaction of people entering a conditioned space. More recent studies based on the reactions of subjects after several hours' exposure to the controlled environment have suggested that relative humidity has a negligible or much smaller effect on the sensation of warmth. These results apply to lightly clothed subjects engaged in light activities. The effects of relative humidity on the comfort of people engaged in moderate to high levels of activity have not been carefully re-examined, but it may be assumed that relative humidity will have a marked influence under conditions of sweating. Low relative humidity may well be undesirable for reasons other
March 24, 1977

than those based on thermal comfort. Low levels will no doubt lead to increased evaporation from the membranes of the nose and throat, and to drying of the skin and hair. Some medical opinion attributes the increased incidence of respiratory complaints to drying out of the mucous membranes due to low humidities indoors in winter. However, no well documented evidence appears to have been presented which would indicate a serious hazard to health resulting from exposure of people to low humidity conditions. In spite of lack of complete information, it seems logical to assume that extremes of humidity are undesirable and that, for human comfort, relative humidities should be kept within a broad range of 30 to 60 percent."
2.	The benefits of humidification are not fully documented. Note response to first question.
3.	No.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the greater part of the substance of the bill relates to the responsibility of my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), clause 5, which has to do with the borrowing authority, comes under my responsibility. I should, therefore, like to make a report to the House on the exercise of borrowing authority in the fiscal year now ending and in the coming year.
In clause 5 of the interim supply bill now before the House the government is seeking a new statutory borrowing authority of $7 billion and to cancel all outstanding and unused borrowing authority. As hon. members are aware, the Financial Administration Act, part IV, section 36, requires that "no money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of Parliament". This refers to "new" money only because there is a continuing authority in the act for the government to borrow funds to repay maturing debt. Authority to borrow sufficient new money to cover estimated financial requirements together with a margin for contingencies is normally sought and granted in one of the first appropriation acts of a new fiscal year.
The long-established procedure for seeking new borrowing powers had been to attach a clause to supply bills brought before the House. This provided no opportunity to debate the borrowing authority being sought under this procedure because the clause is not part of the estimates discussed in standing committees and the supply bill is normally passed without debate.
Mr. Speaker, it was agreed last year that there should be an opportunity for debate on this topic and, indeed, the procedures now being followed reflect a recommendation by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization and agreements among the House leaders.
Hon. members may find it helpful if I begin by reviewing the situation in fiscal 1976-77 which will shortly come to an end. It will be recalled that a borrowing authority of $6 billion was provided in Appropriation Act No. 2, 1976. Under this total authority of $6 billion, we have obtained net new money of $4.85 billion this fiscal year and a further $275 million will be obtained from the April 1 bond issue. Thus, the unused authority which will be cancelled by the passage of this bill will amount to about $875 million. By March 31, 1977, the increases in debt issues will be as follows: treasury bills, $1,760 million; Canada savings bonds, $800 million; marketable bonds, $2,290 million. The total is $4,850 million.
The amounts offered at the 90-day and 180-day treasury bill auctions were $30 million above the amounts maturing each week of the fiscal year. The one-year bills were auctioned four times during the year with increments totalling $200 million over the period. In fiscal 1976-77, $1,960 million marketable bonds matured and $4,250 million new bonds were sold. In order to both broaden the market for our marketable bonds and to lengthen the average term to maturity of our debt, emphasis was placed, during the year, on raising money in the longer term bond market. About 38 per cent of the bonds sold during this period had a maturity in excess of ten years and, as

a result, the average term of the federal debt was lengthened from three years eight months to four years six months.
The 1976-77 Canada savings bond program was most successful in terms of meeting our objectives. Gross sales of about $2,100 million were achieved while redemptions during the fiscal year totalled about $1,300 million. Reflecting our efforts to de-emphasize Canada savings bonds as a source of new funds, Canada savings bonds now represent approximately 38 per cent of the total government debt, as compared with 41 per cent a year ago.
The ownership of the government's debt changed quite significantly during fiscal 1976-77. Chartered banks increased their holdings of marketable securities by about $700 million, or 8.6 per cent, while the Bank of Canada has increased its holdings by about $1,000 million, or 12.5 per cent. The general public, however, increased holdings of government of Canada marketable securities by about $2.3 billion, or 36.8 per cent, as well as increasing holdings of Canada savings bonds by $800 million, or 5.1 per cent.
By March 31, 1977 our cash balances are expected to be standing at a level somewhat higher than the $3.1 billion level recorded at the end of the previous fiscal year. The difference reflects exchange transactions with the Bank of Canada and in the foreign exchange markets. These elements of our balances are extremely volatile and cannot be counted on to provide a permanent contribution toward meeting our cash requirements.
Since the books will remain open for a period of time after the close of the fiscal year, it will be some time before more detailed accounts can be prepared showing the breakdown between budgetary and non-budgetary transactions. I shall be providing the House with some preliminary estimates, however, in my budget. The new statutory borrowing authority of $7 billion will provide a margin for contingencies. In the coming fiscal year, as in most previous years, the full amount of this borrowing authority may not be required. It is important, however, that we have the flexibility properly to plan and implement our debt management operations.

The latest Bank of Canada statistics, of January 12, 1977, indicate that $41,138 million is the debt of Canada. Of this, there was $16,577 million in Canada savings bonds and $24,279 million in various types of papers, bonds, treasury bills, and so on. With particular reference to our estimates, what is of more concern to me is the increase in the size of the estimates to deal with the national debt. In 1966, $1,110 million was required. In 1974 it was $2,608.9 million. In 1975 it had gone to $3,208.4 million. In 1976, up to supplementary estimates A, it was $3,775 million. This year, as it appears at page 82 of the "blue book", we see that the total program for public debt shall cost $5,350 million. This is not an inconsiderable sum of money. One will appreciate these astronomical figures. In other words, I would say that 96 per cent to 97 per cent of the interest that the government of Canada paid on its national debt is payable in Canada. To that extent, it is money that stays at home.
I do not think this could be said entirely with respect to some of the provinces and the provincial Crown agencies which have to pay a great deal of interest abroad. This is not entirely a matter of accident, because I think, because of the annual sales of Canada savings bonds and certain other features of federal bonds, that some of the provincial authorities find themselves entirely crowded out of the Canadian money market. Canadians, under our tax system, have precious little money to invest in Canada savings bonds, RRSPs, life insurance and other forms of investment. Up to 43 per cent of our gross national product is paid directly into public treasuries. This affords very little leeway for savings. Government of Canada bonds are not bought by provincial governments and municipalities: they are competing for money.
Since the so-called 1971 tax reforms the government of Canada, as well as the provinces, has certainly been slicing into the GNP, leaving precious little to the Canadian bond market. It is no wonder that Canadian Crown agencies, governments, the provinces, municipalities, school boards and businesses have to go abroad to tap savings. Our tax system in Canada confiscates earnings to a degree that should be unacceptable to the Canadian public.
One can only do certain things with one's dollars. Either the Canadian government takes them in the form of tax, which naturally is of no benefit to the taxpayer, or the taxpayer is given an opportunity of saving some money and investing it at his own choice either in Canadian bonds or some other form of Canadian investment. Until we learn our lesson we will be forever bleating that there is too much demand on foreign capital to serve legitimate Canadian interests. Frankly, we as Canadians are the authors of our own misfortune because governments both at this level and the provincial level are going in with both hands and ladling up all they can of the Canadian economic pie.
On that count, Mr. Speaker, I hope we will be able in due course to move into committee of the whole, where my colleagues and others in the House will then turn their attention

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage I want to discuss some questions in connection with the energy estimates, but before going into that I would like to record my surprise at parliament's lack of control in these matters, something which I have observed in the brief time I have been here since last November. At least today we have an opportunity to discuss these matters, but I have found that the time we spend in committees on estimates is misspent so far as obtaining answers from ministers is concerned. I have made many attempts to get some information in various committees but I have found my attempts to be futile.
Not only am I surprised at the fact that billions of dollars go through parliament on deadlines without an opportunity being afforded to the opposition to pressure the government in
Interim Supply
connection with the estimates and supplementary supply, but the new rule changes brought in by the government have choked off discussion and limited control by the House in these matters. Also, when questions are asked during the question period they are treated very lightly.
I consider that when Canada faces a grave energy situation-and presumably the government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources feel the same way in this matter-the question must be treated seriously. Heaven only knows that we have had a sufficient number of energy studies, energy strategies, energy policies and initiatives, as well as technical studies in the last three or four years since the energy crisis arose in the fall of 1973. We have had every kind of strategy, initiatives and report that one could expect from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. What we want now is some kind of action from the department in these areas.
Studies were tabled in the House last week which show that energy self-sufficiency in Canada is very unlikely to be achieved. The situation is very serious indeed. Energy costs will escalate. They will certainly double within the next five years or less. Yet when we ask questions in the House regarding these matters we are treated with buffoonery. Hon. members opposite act as if they were gargoyles when they answer questions in the way mine was answered yesterday on this matter. We consider this to be a very serious issue.

subsubtopic: ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1978
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1978
speechtext:
In 1973 the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources initiated all these studies and strategies, and yet they are not being carried out. Only lip service is given to them. Let us consider some of these studies. Let us tike a look, first, at a study entitled, "An Energy Strategy for Canada (Summary)" tabled in the House last Thursday. At page 3 it is stated that these are energy-related targets. These days it is always a target, a policy, an initiative or a strategy. The study reads, at page 3:
The major energy-related targets adopted by the government of Canada are ... to reduce Canadian net dependence on imported oil in 1985 to one-third of our total oil demands.
That will never be achieved under the present initiatives. It goes on to read:
-to double, at a minimum, exploration and development in the frontier areas of Canada over the next three years-
This goes back to 1976 when the study was published. It goes on to read:
-under acceptable social and environmental conditions.
What is happening? The other study tabled last week shows that if Canada is even to attempt to be self-sufficient in oil and gas, and I refer to page 4 of the study entitled "Oil and Natural Gas Resources of Canada, 1976" which reads:
The bulk of the hydrocarbon potential (mainly gas) lies in the three frontier regions, the Mackenzie Delta-Beaufort Sea, Arctic Islands and Labrador Shelf regions which are expensive and difficult to explore.
The other two areas where we have a chance to be self-sufficient are in heavy oils and in the tar sands, both of which will

March 24, 1977
Interim Supply
be very expensive to develop. I attempted to ask a question yesterday about what the minister is doing to expedite frontier exploration. It is stated in the energy strategy study that he will double it over the next three years, but two years have already gone by and we find that not only has the exploration not doubled but it has been decreased by in excess of 50 per cent. In the Arctic Islands the number of oil wells drilled plummetted to 12 last year from the 1973 and 1974 high figures of 23 each year, and the forecast is that there will be a 50 per cent drop in 1977 from last year. In the Mackenzie Delta there is a dramatic drop of 70 per cent from the 1973 peak season of 60 wells, and this year there will be much the same number as in 1976. In other words, the rate has not doubled since the statement was made; it has declined in excess of 50 per cent. Why is that? I will not give you my own opinion as to why. I will give you the opinion from Oil Week in their issue of February 28, a knowledgeable magazine of the industry:
The decline in exploration in the northern frontiers is due to two reasons. In the southern basin, established transportation facilities, good potential... have caused exploration companies to redirect this money to the more favourable areas, and secondly, government waffling, fence-sitting, inaction and indecision on pipelines and land regulations has led to the conclusion that eventual cash flow from Arctic regions may be small.
As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been waffling, sitting on the fence, not acting and indecisive on these questions, we would like some answers from him. Six years ago the oil and gas regulations then in effect were removed and the whole subject was opened up for further exploration. I believe it was on April 27, 1976, that the energy strategy for Canada was made public. It was on May 19, 1976, that the proposed petroleum and natural gas act and the proposed Canadian oil and gas regulations were tabled by the minister, but we are still waiting for the legislation and the regulations to be made public and introduced into the House. That is despite the fact that in the study, "Energy Strategy for Canada", at page 38 it is stated that these regulations would be introduced that year. The following is stated:
Federal legislation concerning Canadian oil and gas land regulations, to be introduced to parliament shortly-
It was practically a year ago that the document was published. Further on in the same document, at page 127, the following statement is made:
-the legislation concerning Canadian oil and gas land regulations that will be presented to parliament this year and that will govern exploration and development activity in areas falling within federal jurisdiction, will impose only a nominal royalty and provide a substantial degree of flexibility.
They have not yet been introduced. Yesterday the minister said "soon", and in the committee last week he also said "soon". People who know something about this say that unless speculation is ended about the terms that will apply, there will be very little exploration in these frontier areas. The fall in exploration levels is not so much due to exploration results as to the result of government inaction. There is no foreseeable production time-frame. That is what has happened. Yesterday, when I attempted to ask a question about whether the government is going to provide an incentive so that these frontier
[Mr. Crosbic.J
areas can be explored more quickly in order to achieve the government's targets, the minister brushed off my question with what I described as a "smart-ass" answer. I made the mistake of using the word "smart".

If the Chairman considers those words to be unparliamentary, I withdraw them. In any event, it was a Smart Alec answer which had nothing to do with what I was asking. If I wanted to ask about the oil and gas regulations of the government of Newfoundland, I would ask the government of Newfoundland; I would not ask the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. We are not here in this House for jokes and byplay-and it is not true to say that I have any connection with anything the government of Newfoundland is doing. I left there seven months ago. I am quite prepared to defend whatever that government did when I was there, but I do not even know what its proposed regime is with regard to these oil and gas regulations. They were set out in the last couple of months.
In any event, that is irrelevant. The minister is in a jurisdictional dispute with the government of Newfoundland as to who has control of these matters, but there is no jurisdictional dispute about frontier areas north of the 60th parallel. That is what I was asking about. The minister should get on with the job of seeing that every action necessary to develop the frontier areas is taken if it is his desire that we be self-sufficient.
Our energy future is grim indeed from the point of view of our being self-sufficient and from the point of view of costs; but all we have are these studies and some very tentative steps. What we need now is action. There have been enough studies. There has been enough ministerial mug-wumping. It is time for the minister to outline what he is going to do, how he is going to do it, what it is going to cost, and what the price of oil and gas will be. His studies show that even when oil and gas prices in Canada rise to the world level, that will not be enough to make new tar sands plants and new heavy oil plants economic, certainly not with the present royalty and taxation regime. What is the minister doing about that?
There is supposed to be a meeting of federal and provincial officials to try to settle the terms of the development of another tar sands project. When will there be a progress report on that? What is happening with regard to heavy oil? What is happening to oil prices? In his studies the minister says that within two to four years those prices will rise to the world level. They have to rise to the world level. The other day, in committee, the minister asked what the policy of the Progressive Conservative party is on that. If he does not already know, I will reassure him that our policy is that the prices for oil and gas have to rise to world level, but that in doing this over a period of time we have to keep prices in the United States as a major factor since we cannot allow our prices to climb higher than theirs for competitive reasons.
March 24, 1977

However, bearing that in mind, we have to go to world prices for oil and gas for conservation reasons and so that we can develop our frontier resources, our tar sands and our heavy oil. But what is the program for that? There is to be a meeting of ministers on April 6. What will be the minister's strategy there? What is holding up the legislation on oil and gas regulations? A year ago the government said the legislation would be introduced in parliament very shortly. What is happening? Nero fiddled while Rome burned, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is giggling, but all our gigawatt hours are being used up and our reserves are burning away.
The minister is not taking our questions seriously. Alberta, British Columbia and, now, even Saskatchewan have changed their revenue regimes. Saskatchewan says it is now going to change its regime to encourage more exploration and development because its past regimes have been too restrictive. That is how the industry has found them to be. What is the government of Canada doing to encourage more exploration in this area? I sometimes think that the minister must be a foreign agent. He should be listed as a lobbyist for East-Can. He keeps referring to East-Can in irrelevant references to the Labrador situation and the dispute with the Newfoundland government.
I have yet to see an oil or gas company which is satisfied with even the regulations proposed by the federal government, much less the regulations of the other government. However, there is no doubt-and experience shows-that if we are going to get under way development in the frontier regions and on the Arctic Islands, and if we are going to do very much with regard to tar sands and heavy oil, there has to be a considerable number of government initiatives.
When the minister speaks I would like him to touch on these energy strategies. They pay lip service to the development of hydro power and renewable energy resources, but lip service only. Each of these documents has the same kind of thing to say about hydro energy and about how it must be encouraged, yet the government of Canada has gone backward in the last six or eight years by not encouraging the development of hydro resources in Canada. I am not just referring to Labrador, although in Labrador alone, if our hydro resources were developed and if they were used in Newfoundland and Canada generally, there would be a tremendous saving: there would be 44.3 million barrels of electricity generating oil saved if Gull Island, Muskrat Falls, the Eagle and several other rivers were developed, and another 38 million barrels of oil would be saved if the hydro potential of five rivers running from Labrador through Quebec to the gulf were developed.
I am not talking just about Labrador. Hydro energy can be found in many remote locations, but it is expensive. There are many other areas throughout Canada where hydro can still be developed, although they are remote northern areas. That potential can be found in the Yukon and in British Columbia. In northwestern Ontario there are rivers which flow to James Bay and to Hudson Bay. There is the Mackenzie River, and rivers running to Ungava Bay. There is the Great Bear River near Norman Wells, the Rat River near the Mackenzie Delta,
Interim Supply
the Liard River, the Yukon River in the Yukon and in northern British Columbia, and so forth. There are other potential sites in British Columbia. Hydro sites are not just to be found in Labrador, but the hydro potential which is available is remote and expensive and it will not be developed unless the government of Canada is forthcoming with a more generous policy of financial assistance.
Six or seven years ago, in Manitoba, the policy was that the government would lend 100 per cent of the cost of transmission lines from the Nelson River development, but the policy today is to lend a provincial utility engaged in a project involving interregional or interprovincial connections 50 per cent of the money at Crown corporation interest rates. The policy has gone backwards, even though the need is now much greater. The policy of helping nuclear developments is much more generous. The policy is to provide a 50 per cent loan for the first plant in a province, but the government is heavily subsidizing heavy water, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the development of nuclear energy in every direction. Meanwhile, hydro energy, which is renewable, clean and which has no dangers associated with it, receives this half-hearted federal support which is nothing but lip service.
What is the matter with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources? Is the minister blind to the use and the virtues of hydro development? Has it something to do with the fact that the only river he is familiar with is the Humber River which flows through Toronto? Why cannot a real policy of hydro development be initiated by the government of Canada?
In reply to a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Central Nova, the minister said that he is taking a new initiative with the province of Newfoundland for Labrador. If that is so, it is a very low-key initiative. There have been no substantive new offers from the federal government with regard to hydroelectric development in Newfoundland for Gull Island. There should be. It is criminal that development is not under way there now, but as yet there has not been developed-and there should be-a general hydro assistance policy with much more generous terms than the present one. If Canada is going to get anywhere, we need a new hydro assistance policy.
Lip service has also been paid to the matter of energy conservation. All the strategies and documents suggest that the government hopes to reduce growth to 3.5 per cent per year. As long as politics intervene there is no chance of that, because any genuine conservation assistance will go only to certain selected provinces, depending on what governments those provinces have and depending upon political factors, but not on reason or logic at all.
There are a lot of questions that should be asked in this area and I suggest to the minister that he should deal with some of the major issues today. The documents he has tabled are a major indictment of his inaction. The ordinary people do not understand what they are going to be hit with in the next five to ten years or that what they are going to pay for energy will

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few general remarks by way of introduction and then permit members to put specific questions. I think all hon. members have been entertained by the rhetoric of the hon. member opposite. When I made the charge yesterday that he was the author of the Newfoundland regulations, I did not realize that I had hit home so accurately. I can place no other interpretation upon the very substantial part of his remarks this evening which have been directed to defence of the position of Newfoundland and the freedom of Newfoundland to impose its own set of regulations regardless of the price to Newfoundland and regardless of the price to Canadians.
That was the most disappointing part of his remarks. Newfoundland is often regarded-and I think is probably claimed by the hon. member-as one of the poorer regions of the country. It is also a province that has on its offshore some of the richest potential oil and natural gas resources in the country. Six wells have been drilled in some of the toughest water anywhere in the world, and indications of petroleum and natural gas have been found in three of those six wells. That must be regarded as unique in this country and in the northern regions of the offshore. It is very encouraging, and any oilman will endorse that. It is also a fact that drilling in this area has only a three-month season because the icebergs move down and the rigs have to move off. It is dangerous to the drillers and dangerous environmentally, to extend the season. It is also in deep water.

Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Regional Economic Expension for this year, like the last two years, scarcely keep up with the inflation factor in this country. In my opinion, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is largely a failure in terms of its stated goal to eliminate the disparity in income gaps as between the Atlantic provinces and central Canada or the Canadian average income. So much of the DREE funds each year, including this year, are allocated to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario that DREE has become a sort of farce in so far as closing the income gap between the Atlantic region and central Canada is concerned.
DREE in the modern period had its genesis with the study that was done by Walter Gordon in 1957 in which he advocated for the Atlantic provinces that a capital projects commission be established. This was shortly to be followed by the Atlantic Development Board which consisted largely of infrastructure expenditures in the Atlantic provinces in the nature of power and highways. It was supposed to come up with a plan for development of the Atlantic provinces that would gradual-

ly, over a period of years, close the interim gap that is so old and so consistent within Canadian confederation. The Atlantic Development Board folded before it came up with a plan. It was rapidly followed by another alphabetical agency, the Area Development Agency. It, too, folded after a few years.
In 1969 we got the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion has followed a policy of developing the larger or metropolitan areas of Atlantic provinces, practically ignoring the smaller ones. There are gaps between the regions within a province; for example, between metropolitan Saint John, New Brunswick, and northern New Brunswick, between St. John's, Newfoundland, and all the outer regions of Newfoundland, between Charlottetown and the rest of the province of Prince Edward Island, and between the Halifax-Dartmouth area and the rest of the province of Nova Scotia.
What we have is a policy that is based upon the notion that where there is already a government apparatus in the form of an existing government, for example in Nova Scotia which is highly supplemented by the defence sector, the policy is to push large funds in infrastructure into these areas while at the same time allowing the outer areas to go down relative to these central areas. The result is that only recently, with the advent of the Anti-Inflation Board and the cutting down of federal expenditures in areas such as Halifax-Dartmouth, has the gap been somewhat closed between the Atlantic provinces and the central Canadian average. However, this was at the cost of the outer areas. What DREE has done is look after three-quarters of a million of the people in the Atlantic provinces while completely neglecting the other VA million who live there. I suggest that this is a stupid policy.
If I were a Liberal member from the Atlantic provinces I would ask the cabinet to reconsider whether what they are doing in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is largely a waste of time except for image building. They can say they have a Department of Regional Economic Expansion. When Premier Regan took over in the province of Nova Scotia, rather than completely throwing out the voluntary economic planning board that had been set up by a previous Conservative government, he left it in order to show that they had the image of a planning power. Something much more decisive is needed. I do not have time to go into detail. However, in my opinion one of the great failures of DREE as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned is related to the general fiscal and monetary policies that have been followed by this government in recent years, especially the so-called Trudeau years.
Today there is a pessimistic feeling that we can never really get back to full employment in this country. Why? It is because of the monetary and fiscal policies that have been followed for so long. We have a classic example of that now with over one million Canadians unemployed. If you include the hidden unemployed, it would be no exaggeration to say that there are between 1,300,000 and 1,500,000. All of this has been done in order to control inflation. At the same time, we have had tight control over the private sector by means of the
March 24, 1977

Anti-Inflation Board. In my opinion, there was no need for it. A correction was probably needed to balance off the public sector wages in the past five or eight years against the private sector. Rather than the government facing up to that responsibility-and this includes not only the federal government but provincial and municipal governments-they Jet the whole situation get out of line.
The failure of DREE is closely related to the failure of national policies. We will never get a successful Department of Regional Economic Expansion and a closing of the income gap between the Atlantic provinces and other poorer regions of Canada and the other regions that are well off until there is co-ordination between the fiscal and monetary macroeconomic policies and the policies co-ordinated with new development organizations at a regional level.
As I have pointed out, there are many today who are saying that we can never get back to full employment. With the proper policies we can get back to it within three or four years. There is a pessimistic feeling that we can never really get back to a full employment economy. I propose in this speech to show that it can, and must, be done in order to keep confederation going.
We are worried, now, about the cultural climate of Quebec because of the victory of the Parti Quebecois which is connected with separatism. We know there are linguistic and cultural roots. The feeling of separatism and the kindling of that feeling in Quebec is largely tied to the fact that their economic resources have not been used well. Many of their people, both young and old, who should be working are not working. According to Statistics Canada, there is 10 per cent unemployment in that province, but in reality it is closer to 13 per cent. That, in itself, is enough to kindle the separatist feeling. All this has happened under a man well-intentioned in his bilingual policy, although it has been badly implemented, but who has completely neglected to manage our economy so well that these forces in Quebec could be squelched. I feel, coming from the Atlantic region, complete affinity for these people as far as this economic insecurity and this feeling of economic inferiority is concerned, because really what the government has failed to do in managing its over-all policy is to allow Quebec, the Atlantic regions and northern Ontario, and so on, to suffer in order that the large metropolitan areas would improve.
It is true that most people in this country live in the large metropolitan areas, and it is true that the government-and this bothers me very much-has a policy for the future based upon a policy that has been shown in the United States to be stupid, to build very large-huge-cities so that you never contain, for example, a population of the size of Toronto; you just let it go on and on, because you let market forces keep intervening because you cannot take the steps to halt them as a government; and provincial governments seem to agree. It is the same in Montreal, the same in Vancouver. So we are content to say, as Canadians, that within the next 20 or 25
Interim Supply
years, three-quarters of our people will live in four or five cities.
No wonder there is a feeling of alienation. No wonder there is a feeling of separatism outside these areas, when most of the government's thinking is done this way and when you have a kind of a bone thrown to the dog in terms of something called DREE that does nothing except add to that type of thing by just improving the large metropolitan areas of the Atlantic region.
Again, if you look at the statistics, Mr. Chairman, you will find that outside Halifax and Dartmouth in Nova Scotia, outside Saint John and Fredericton in New Brunswick, outside St. John's in Newfoundland, outside Charlottetown in Prince Edward Island, the rest of the people in the Atlantic region get only 50 per cent-between 50 per cent and 55 per cent-of the average income of Canadians who live in the other metropolitan areas I have mentioned, especially here in central Canada, in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. I submit this is a disgrace and that we need policies of a national nature that will make regional organizations such as DREE meaningful only when they are co-ordinated so that they will have some kind of meaning for these outlying areas. Until this is done, until we get these policies, until we get a recommitment for full employment, there is no hope that what I am asking for will take place. In other words, we need the pursuit of equity in this country through guaranteed employment.
Everybody in Canada, left, right and centre, would probably say they are in favour of an equitable society. The difference arises as to what exactly is meant by equity and the divergent evaluation of the costs and benefits in conflicting ways of achieving equity. Since in our democratic country society's idea of fair distribution of economic resources depends upon bringing together our various individual ideas of equity, the first problem is to determine how each of us wpuld specify an equitable society. Only then can we move on to determining and implementing our collective wisdom.
To aid in this process I invite hon. members to perform the following experiment called, in psychology, the Gedanken experiment. Imagine that all economic resources were to be awarded in a random lottery where none of us would know whether we were to gain the largest or the smallest prize. If this were the case, what distribution of prizes would we like our lottery to make? While we might agree on the amount of inequality we would be willing to generate, most of us would not advocate great inequalities, and all of us would be in favour of some minimum prize-our survival would depend on it. Those advocating inequality must prove that any decrease in inequality would reduce the size or rate of growth of the economic pie that is available for distribution.
Given this burden of proof, what does the evidence show? Fortunately, this is one of the few cases where in North America all the empirical evidence points in the same direction. Surveys of work behaviour, econometric studies of work decisions and negative income tax experiments all suggest that current inequalities are much larger than those necessary to produce and expand the gross national product. Just how thorough is the inequality in the distribution of the national economic pie? In 1965, as far as family units were concerned, the bottom 20 per cent were getting 4.4 per cent of that pie while the top 20 per cent were getting 41.4 per cent. The family unit is defined here as including both families and unattached individuals. In 1974, the bottom 20 per cent were getting 4 per cent of the national pie and the top 20 per cent were getting 42.5 per cent. The sad part of the matter is that both in Canada and the United States the relative position of these groups has been the same since 1957, despite all the individual components which go to make up the welfare state in a mixed capitalistic system.
When you look at families, and that includes the unattached individual, you find that in 1965 the bottom 20 per cent were getting 6.2 per cent of the pie and the top 20 per cent were getting 39 per cent. In 1974 it was 6.3 per cent for the bottom 20 per cent and 38.8 per cent for the top 20 per cent. In 1974, there were 5.5 million families in Canada. We dismiss this fact and try to hide behind the statistics. But they are Canadian citizens and families.
There were, in 1974, 93,500 families who received less than $3,000 a year in this country. There are some, of course, who are quick to point out that these statistics need to be qualified. For example, it is pointed out that the lowest income group, who get such a miserable morsel of our economic pie, are not a permanent group but change from generation to generation. In the economists' parlance, they are a flow and not a stock. This argument seems to me to take nothing away from the argument that the lowest 20 per cent, so heavily made up of senior citizens and women who are heads of households, are suffering very badly under our economic system.

I think in all fairness that we must recognize and respect provincial jurisdictions. I would have preferred that the hon.

member speak in a non-partisan way. The question is not whether Nova Scotia's provincial administration is Liberal or not, or whether New Brunswick's is Progressive Conservative or not. The basic question is far too serious to stop at partisan considerations. Be that as it may, it is apparent that since the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established by Parliament in July 1969, disparities have been getting worse in New Brunswick, between the richer areas in the south, including the cities of St. John, Moncton and Fredericton for instance, and the northern areas including to all practical purposes the rest of the province. This is why I am very much concerned, as is the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan). Certainly he can speak with much eloquence and conviction for his province of Nova Scotia, and I commend him for that. But I feel we must not enter into partisan considerations.
This leads me to suggest it is more urgent than ever that provincial governments in the Atlantic area and the national government here in Ottawa, and especially the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) sit down and develop together a plan to tackle regional disparities effectively and efficiently, taking into account the needs of all parts of the area, and putting and end once and for all to the injection of millions and hundreds of millions of dollars into the already thriving centres he referred to, as Halifax, St. John, N.B., St. John's, and Charlottetown.
