Mr. Chairman, may I take this opportunity in the time allotted to me to return to the energy situation. I wish to express to the minister our appreciation for accommodating members on this side of the House by being here and having his officials present to listen to our side of the story and possibly answer what we think are some very pressing questions. I intend to indulge in a short discussion this afternoon which will add an entirely new dimension to the energy question, new at least to the minister and his department though certainly not new to those of us who have always been looking at energy policies which are designed for the future, having looked back to the past and evaluated what has been happening in the field of energy production and consumption.
I look on the government and this particular department as a group of crisis managers. I call them crisis reactors. "An Energy Strategy for Canada" was, of course, the result of the energy crisis of 1973, when we woke up one morning and found that our fossil energy reserves were not at all what the government and most of us, including industry, had perceived them to be. It is obvious to me, as it is to most people, that the
Interim Supply
need is for a long-term energy policy. By that I mean that we have to plan 25 years ahead. In order to do that, we must also look back 25 years to get a realistic picture not only of where we will stand 25 years hence but what type of energy we will be using at that time, and beyond, and the price we will be paying for that commodity.
In order to put that picture into focus, Mr. Chairman, one would have to take account of the total global community. I would be naive in the extreme to think that over that period of time Canada could plan its own energy strategy in total isolation and be able jealously to guard its reserve in isolation. One would have to take into account the present rate of growth in the world. There are presently four billion people in the global community; 25 years from now or by the turn of the next century there will be roughly 6.5 billion people.
It is only reasonable to assume that all these people will have achieved a much better standard of living, much closer to that of our own, and that to achieve any kind of breakthrough in the development of the third world and improve the standard of living in some of the underdeveloped countries massive amounts of energy will be required. It seems that the kind of lifestyle which we enjoy depends on gadgetry and the energy required for same. Canadians today are second only to the United States in the consumption of energy. Each family in Canada consumes roughly 55 barrels of oil every year. In projecting 25 years ahead we must take account of the fact that over the past 25 years consumption of energy by Canadians has tripled. Oil and gas 25 years ago met one-quarter of our total energy needs. Today they fill two-thirds of our requirements.
One of the first stages of a long-term energy policy would have to be a policy of conservation. I compliment the minister and his officials for at least recognizing that terminology. I am not at all enthusiastic about the early signs of his conservation policy. I do not believe that these primitivists in our society today are really serious when it comes to turning off the lights and turning down the thermostat. They let their hair grow and say that we have to return to a more primitive lifestyle, but if they were really put to the test I do not think they would be serious.
Furthermore, I do not think we would be as aggressive as the minister likes to tell us to be in turning off our lights at home and turning down our thermostats. Domestic requirements for energy are not really all that great. What we need to be doing, and what the essence of a conservation policy must be, is that our industries and our cities have to learn to convert some of the industrial and solid wastes. It is estimated by the minister's officials that every year we are wasting roughly as much energy as we consume. If trends which have been set over the past 25 years continue, and there is no reason to believe they will not-the trends I am talking about are the increase in our population and our treatment of energy reserves-25 years from now we will be consuming four times as much energy as we do today.
I think that puts into focus the kind of picture I am hoping to portray, namely, that in terms of the global community-

March 24, 1977
Interim Supply
our own energy requirements and the requirements of North America 25 years from now-it should be quite obvious to anyone, and it is no great challenge to the imagination, to come to the conclusion that this globe and its fossil reserves will not be sustaining the demand on its inventory past the year 2000.
The obvious questions are: Where will we go, and what will we do? This government will likely wait until the crisis becomes real and more people indulge in deeper examination of the whole question. Then we will react to a crisis situation and implement all kinds of programs which not only will be very costly in human terms but in most cases will be irreversible in terms of the environmental and ecological penalties which we will have to pay.
I have a 14 year-old son, Mr. Chairman, who the other day wrote an essay in school. I suppose he got his information from an encyclopedia that one could go to, but the theme of his essay was that the sun, solar energy, would likely be the answer. As I say, he is only 14 years old and he says this in his essay, which I think is quite a compliment to him:
The most colossal dynamo of all is the sun, an unimaginably vast source of power which directly or indirectly affects everything on earth. If all the world's fuels were gathered in one place and burned at a rate to match the sun, they would be consumed in four days.
Although the sun is overcoming a distance of 93 million miles, if trapped, would be enough power to sufficiently supply the earth for over a year, in only two minutes! Considering the amount of energy available from the sun, man has been surprisingly unsuccessful in obtaining it.
What I am getting at, Mr. Chairman, is that this government has done nothing at all, or very little, to look ahead and examine some of the options that we will have to consider in the year 2000 and beyond.
A joint conference in which 13 countries took part was held in Winnipeg last year. The conference looked at solar energy in particular. Our scientists and officials attended. The American contribution to the conference was well founded and well documented, and their solar energy program was well planned. By the year 2000 they plan to draw from the sun 70 per cent of their needs. Over the next two years they have committed $260 million to solar energy development. If they were to make a firm commitment of the type they made to send a man to the moon, I say that in the next ten years there will be no energy shortage because between us we will have developed the technology to harness energy from the sea of energy in which we bathe every day.
One of our leading scientists at the conference showed a blank slide on the projection screen to portray the total amount of our research in the coming year in the field of solar energy. If we continue this approach to renewable resources, we will have to continue to rely on other countries, as we do in other fields of scientific endeavour, to produce the technology that is required to harness these new modes of energy. Also we will have to rely on these countries to produce the technology required to convert energy.
(Mr. Oberlc.]
The conference concerned itself also with cost comparisons. We all know what it will cost to bring to market the conventional reserves on which we rely under this government's long range energy policy. In comparison with the cost of renewable resources, the cost of conventional reserves will skyrocket every year as we push farther back to the frontiers, to the Mackenzie Valley and the Beaufort Sea. It will cost more and more every year as we convert heavy oil and tar sands, and there will be a steady increase to our consumers as our prices reach the level of world prices. In contrast with that, the kind of technology that is now being developed to harness solar energy will cost the most at first, but as it is used and refined, and as we convert our homes to the use of this kind of energy, the price will drop. There are no penalties to pay in environmental or ecological terms for the use of the energy which nature provides for us, and there is no limit to that resource in terms of renewable energy reserves.
The minister's officials estimate that capital requirements for the remainder of the 1970's will be $40 billion to $68 billion. Of course this will have to be recovered with the marketing of our oil. If we close our borders to foreign countries, Canadians will have to pay back the $40 billion to $68 billion. The energy policy for Canada indicates the spread in these huge amounts. In the $40 billion component, if we were actually to achieve a conservation program, we would be using less energy in the next two years. Then in the $50 billion program we would use about equal amounts to those we have been using recently. In the $68 billion program we would build the Mackenzie Valley pipeline and several of the infrastructures which will be required to bring the frontier reserves to market.
I would like to hear the minister's response to my remarks when I conclude them. In view of the fact that he is such a proponent of Petro-Canada and of public involvement in the field of energy, I would like him to tell us whether he has asked his officials to estimate how much of the $68 billion will have to come from the public purse to be channeled into this field. Our forecasters estimate that from 1975 to 1990 we will have to come up with $31,000 per family to satisfy our energy requirements. Even solar energy is cheaper today. Surely solar energy, wind energy, and energy from the sea have been intended for man to use, but we have always taken the easy way out.
The minister made a critical comment about my colleague who said that the National Energy Board and the government are procrastinating in making decisions. Let me point out that it was a Tory government which had the first energy policy that ever existed. It was a Tory government which created the National Energy Board. It was Tory policy that established a two-price system-the first policy ever in existence in Canada so far as energy is concerned. It has allowed us to bring oil from the Middle East and Venezuela to our eastern shores, and has allowed us at the same time to harvest and develop our reserves in Canada and to protect our markets. The two-price system was certainly acceptable to eastern Canadians so long as the western price was higher than off-shore prices. But as
March 24, 1977

soon as these prices reached the same level, we soon found the means to equalize oil prices in Canada, and this government has learned to concern itself with energy matters.
Against the background of a long range energy policy, which takes into account that after the year 2,000 we can no longer rely on conventional reserves and will have to develop a new technology that will give us access to the renewable resources around us, we need to catalogue the remaining reserves we have. We need to know every cubic foot of gas and every barrel of oil that are in the ground, and how expensive it will be to market them. In the short term we must be very aggressive in defining our policies with regard to cataloguing our reserves. But then we must learn to plan the period of transition because it will take us 25 years to change our lifestyle and the economic and industrial strategies which we now have.
The most significant segment of our economy is related to the energy field, to the automotive industry, the gasoline marketing industry, and so on, and it will take at least 25 years to plan an orderly transition to allow different economic and demographic strategies to evolve. What is our government doing? It has not even recognized the fact that this kind of thing is necessary, never mind getting to work on it and doing something about it. When can we expect the minister to address himself to this very serious problem?
The problem is that all the policy announcements which come from the government are based on statistical information which is four or five years old; for example, the statistical information we have with regard to the government's intention to channel certain percentages of the available moneys to research. Phase one of "An Energy Policy for Canada' states that we intend to spend 70.6 per cent of our research dollars in the nuclear field and 13.4 per cent on coal. I assume that has to do with some type of coal-gasification or liquefaction for quicker conversion to energy. Oil and gas are to receive 10.6 per cent, and electrical 4.2 per cent. There will be 1 per cent spent on the tar sands, and the others will receive 1 per cent.
I see that my time has elapsed, Mr. Chairman, but I hope you will allow me to make a final comment. The initial priorities for energy research and development must be addressed to fossil fuels. These are the resources which Canada will rely upon to carry it through this century and into the age of nuclear fusion and other advanced technologies. If that is the case, what will we do when we need nuclear fusion and other advanced technology, and who will do the research, if not ourselves? Surely to God we cannot rely on Third World countries, and forever be parasites on the scientific community of the rest of the world.

seems to me there is an excellent opportunity through the work of this committee for members on all sides of the House to discuss the vital issues which affect Canadians in the field of energy.
We sought and obtained very general terms of reference that relate to the entire energy strategy report tabled in this House last spring by the minister. We have held two or three meetings in connection with that report but have had to leave it in order to deal with the matter of the estimates. I will mention a few of these areas, Mr. Speaker. We hope, subject to discussion within the steering committee in the near future, to deal with the question of energy conservation which is probably the single most important area of our entire energy strategy. No matter what we do about future development, figures reported to us recently indicate that by the year 1990 world-wide we will be consuming as much oil in one year as the entire production of the North Sea area. It is extremely important that we bear this in mind.
People are concerned about whether we are actually facing energy shortages or not. Various figures are produced from time to time, but we have to deal with the information at hand, so at the present time it would seem to be the case that by 1990, unless conservation measures are brought in and made an important issue throughout the world, the world will be consuming something in the order of 27 billion barrels of oil. That is a little more than the entire discovery of the North Sea area over a 15-year period. In four months we will be consuming the entire production of the northern slope of Alaska, which is about 10 billion barrels. It has been suggested there should be special committees, but our committee can deal with it. There is nothing like going to the tar sands site to see the difference between mining oil, which is done at the tar sands, and obtaining it through drilling operations. As the hon. member for Scarborough West has so well indicated, the Post Office as a government department is dependent on other departments in order to achieve certain of its responsibilities. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that the buildings we occupy are either leased or built by the Department of Public Works. In our negotiations through collective agreements with our unions we have to receive the authorization, really the delegated authority, from Treasury Board. We are dealt with as a government department. That is the way it has been for some time.
Post Office departments in other jurisdictions have attempted to remove themselves from the grip of government bureaucracy. To date the experience in other areas has not been that encouraging. Those difficulties that the Post Office in Canada has had, and there have been some, have also been those of other jurisdictions. I call the hon. member's attention to decentralization in Great Britain and Germany, as well as in the United States.
In the United States, and I owe this information to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, notwithstanding the attempt to remove the Post Office from the political arena, the impression that one is left with in the United States is that the Post Office is still part and parcel of the government institution. So long has the tradition been in Canada of having the Post Office responsible to the political process that it would take more than one generation, even if a decision were made to have a Crown corporation, for the public to be persuaded that the

political process was not somehow involved in the postal service.
The situation is such that in our present economic context, as hon. members know from the estimates that have been tabled in the House, we are facing a deficit of somewhere in the vicinity of $671 million, more than 50 per cent of the total cost of operation of the Post Office. Having that sort of deficit, it would be very difficult to persuade the Canadian taxpayer that the political process and the post office, which is supported to such a large degree by the public treasury, ought not to be responsible through this particular institution.

He is subject to Treasury Board, to the Department of Labour for labour relations, to Supply and Services for purchases, to Public Works for buildings, and so forth. This is why, in a question I asked the other afternoon, I urged the Postmaster General to seize the initiative and to get all these groups together, because after all it is his ultimate responsibility to come to grips with these matters.
There has been a process of managerial decentralization carried out. It has not been decentralization in the real sense of the word but merely a process of adding yet another tier of executive responsibility. There is no consultation, there is no delegation of authority, and there is no real communication between the regional offices and the national office.
I was talking about rotation of postmasters general in the past few years. Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, the same process seems to be going on with deputy postmasters general because Mr. John MacKay, who was deputy postmaster general from 1969 until recently, has now moved on to the Department of Public Works. I had the privilege of attending a farewell reception for Mr. MacKay, and judging from the tributes which were paid he had done an outstanding job and just seemed to be getting his teeth into some of the major areas of concern, such as the labour problem with which it had taken so long to come to grips.
Interim Supply
I have visited some post office plants in company with a few of my colleagues across Canada and been impressed with the quality of the labour force in the Post Office. Some 50 per cent of them are women and, as they say, our best men are women. Having talked to the employees on the floor, I discovered that the cause of this backlog of 1,200 grievances to which I referred is the little things, such as failure to deal with personal, human problems; failure on the part of supervisors and shop stewards to consult and deal with a difficulty when it arises on the floor of the plant.
What is needed in the Post Office is a wailing wall where people can get things off their chests. Perhaps we need what many modern industries have these days, a chaplain where personal problems can be dealt with. What is needed is a facility to meet human relations.
The mechanization and automation program has been carried on with unwise haste. This has resulted in delays in the opening of some of the major plants, particularly the bulk mailing plant at Mississauga. It has also produced unnecessary labour difficulties, particularly in the Toronto area. The Post Office has a major problem on its plate at the present time with respect to the long delay of up to two years in the opening of the bulk mailing plant in Mississauga because its chosen company to produce the computers to operate the bulk mailing plant, Computing Devices, has not been able to deliver.
I should like the Postmaster General to comment on how he is going to get around this difficulty. Our opposition post office committee was in the Mississauga plant just before Christmas, and it was a crying shame to see a vast area which should have been humming with activity, having been mechanized and automated, occupied by manual sorters who were attempting to cope with the accumulation of mail during the pre-Christmas rush period. The delay must have been costly, and perhaps it is one of the major reasons why the President of the Treasury Board is not able to bring Post Office costs under control. This is another indication that action is urgently needed, and I trust the Postmaster General will come to grips with that specific problem.
Reference has been made to the Post Office service in the United States. I was there last week and I was pleased to see that they are gradually solving some of their difficulties.

No. So far as mechanization in Toronto is concerned, we have three plants in operation. The mechanized plants are in operation save and except the bulk facility in Mississauga. That has nothing to do with labour relations; that delay was caused by one contractor in that particular plant. I would invite the hon. gentleman to visit that plant. The Mississauga plant is really the most sophisticated postal plant. The difficulty is that there is some slight delay owing to a decision made to centralize the computer activity for the whole plant in one central computer. This had not been done before and there are difficulties in this regard. To obviate these difficulties we have decided to use the more orthodox process of using varius computers for various procedures, and in this way we have now completely transferred operations from terminal A to the three mechanized postal plants in Toronto. Within six weeks I am sure the hon. gentleman will join me in congratulating the Post Office staff on having transferred with as little inconvenience as possible under the circumstances.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, perhaps in my initial remarks I did use too much levity. We are not here to joke about the Post Office but to talk about an essential service in Canada. It is a federal institution which serves every Canadian citizen on a regular basis. It is true that it has been the butt end of a number of jokes, but I think this is completely unjustified. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris will agree with me that a great part of the criticism which has befallen the Post Office is unjustified.
In the early days, as the hon. member knows, the Post Office was the only mode of communication in Canada. In those days we had to traverse the country by railway, ox cart, or whatever means of transportation was available. There was no expectation of next day delivery. Today the Post Office is competing with modern communications technology, technology which produces instantaneous results. It is evident that within that particular context the Post Office will fare badly in

comparison. But in terms of the Post Office which the hon. member knew in his early years, today's Post Office is a most efficient and modern institution. As a matter of fact, by 1978, after our mechanization process is completed, we in Canada will have the most sophisticated and reliable postal service in any place in the world.
When the hon. gentleman tells me that the American system is better than ours, I say to him, fie, because that is completely inaccurate. I have visited postal installations in the United States and so has the hon. member, and they do not compare in any way with the sophisticated institutions that the Canadians have developed here. Surely the hon. gentleman should at least admit to his own pride in the high technology involved in our postal code system.

subsubtopic: ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1978
speechtext:
There are other things even more important than the Post Office. We are in danger of imposing a grievous burden on future generations. I refer to the question of the proposed purchase of fighter aircraft at a price estimated at present of $2 billion. Their design, I take it, is for double duty purposes. First of all, in North America we are told we will have a long range interceptor aircraft, and also we will use them in Europe in various roles that I do not need to go into now. I do want to talk about the question of whether these fighter aircraft are needed or are not needed to defend North America. When I questioned the Minister of National Defence about this, he said with a kindly smile that they were designed to protect Canadian security. But I am afraid he is getting into bad habits from the company he is keeping. He did not begin to answer the question which I put to him, which was: how is Canadian security affected by this particular purchase?
I urge that we take a long and careful look at the military needs before we launch on an expensive venture such as the spending of $2 billion, which is the initial figure. We know from long experience that such figures usually multiply. At least that amount of money is supposed to be spent, and I suggest that we take a long and careful look at our military needs. I appreciate that this is a capital expenditure which will be spread over a number of years, but I also recall that it comes on top of $1 billion spent on long range patrol aircraft which were sold to us by Lockheed.
What is the purpose of a fighter aircraft so far as north America is concerned? These new aircraft are to replace the Voodoos which were designed to shoot down manned bombers which would attack Canada, presumably from a source in Europe such as the U.S.S.R. We all agree now that the Voodoos are obsolete, but I suggest that the substitute in defence, the new proposal, is equally obsolete because it is aimed at a non-existent threat. The fact of the matter is that any attack by manned bombers-and this includes the new proposed Backfire which is a medium range bomber which can be refueled to be a long range bomber-on Canada or North America would telegraph its punch, would give advance knowledge of the proposed attack, two or three hours before the weapons arrived, and we have on this continent the power to retaliate massively long before the bombers reached our
Interim Supply
shores. Indeed, most of the targets would disappear long before, and a massive retaliation could be launched and would be available which would completely and utterly destroy the U.S.S.R. as a society.
We live in a missile age, and some people have not caught up with that. They have an idea that a group of bombers coming over from one side can be shot down on the other side, which makes no sense at all in a missile age. We have to assume the sanity of those who might become military opponents, and who amongst the people in those countries would contemplate making an attack on North Amercia or, indeed, on Canada, which would invite their own annihilation?
We are told that this is necessary for deterrence. How much deterrence do we need? The world has surplus deterrents, enough to wipe out the people in both the super powers over and over again, and yet we are supposed to add this extra deterrent of being able to strike down a bomber which might come over to this country, in the face of the fact that we could create a situation in which the use of nuclear retaliation would be almost completely inevitable.
It is sometimes said, as I have mentioned, that this is for deterrence. To my mind that is an argument which makes no sense whatever. We must determine what is the most effective deterrent, whether we have it and whether anything we do or spend is adding one iota to the strength of our deterrents, and I suggest that the constant building up of the ability, to respond to a manned bomber attack, which will probably never happen, is a form of deterrence which is an utter and complete waste of money.
I would like to examine what we could do if we could save a large part of this $2 billion. I do not deny that there is some use for interceptors. We have to defend our sovereignty against casual intervention either in our air space or over our territorial waters, but we certainly do not need 120 or 160 up-to-date fighter aircraft to perform that particular function. The purpose of this large number of fighter aircraft, as I said, is to repel a large scale attack by manned bombers on North America or Canada. When we are talking about how much we could save if we scaled down this colossal sum, I suggest that we always underestimate the total amount required to carry out this kind of plan. My argument is that we should adjust the purchase to the actual need. That indeed is the essence of sound planning of defence policy.
It has been suggested that there is a counter attraction in the possibility of procurement in Canada. Of the six suppliers with whom we are supposed to be dealing four are American, one, I believe, is British, and the other is French. We have absolutely no arrangement, and may never have any arrangement, for procurement in Canada. Indeed when the matter came up before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence this morning, I asked some of our senior officials, and they said there was no assurance, no knowledge or even a tentative assessment or estimate of the amount of

March 24, 1977
Interim Supply
procurement in Canada which will result from expenditure of this sum of about $2 billion.
I would like us to consider-because this is not an impractical subject-what we could do if we did not spend that amount of money on this kind of expenditure. We could use $2 billion in a number of areas. 1 am not suggesting we could use it for all of them. One area is direct job creation. Capital works, both federal and provincial, are needed in such areas as urban transit, which has been promised, schools, hospitals, nursing homes, and parks. We need money for housing for low income Canadians, and we need it to buy insulation to save energy. We could use it-and we would use it-to increase pensions for senior citizens and to reduce the age eligibility to below 65. We could use it-and we need to use it-to cut personal income tax.
We cannot have it both ways. We cannot spend our money on useless hardware and at the same time spend it on the social needs of the people of Canada. There are specific items. During the last election the Prime Minister promised an urban transit subsidy of $290 million. That is part of it, but I think the major area is direct job creation. It is estimated that we could create 200,000 to 250,000 jobs and reduce the unemployment rate from 7.9 per cent, seasonally adjusted, to about 5 per cent.
It is highly practical to suggest that we spend our money on things which are needed. We do not have infinite options. We cannot go on spending money which is wasted and at the same time do the things we need to do.
I do not blame Canadians or particularly the Canadian government. This form of insanity is pervading the whole world. Humanity as a whole is travelling down the road to disaster. We have distorted priorities. We spend $300 billion per year on armaments and other military expenses of that sort. The developing countries, as well as the great powers, spend money in this way. We spend a fraction of that amount dealing with starvation and abject poverty throughout the world. As human beings we are totally misusing the resources we have. We have the ability to deal with human poverty, but we use available money to pile up absolutely fantastic powers of destruction of humanity as a whole.
I am afraid that we in Canada too are in the process of having our attitude softened up by what General Eisenhower described as a military-industrial complex. We are told what we must restrain ourselves, but we are not supposed to restrain ourselves when it comes to extra defence capital expenditures. We in this House do not even go into them. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence does not go into them. The Department of National Defence does not really tell us how necessary those expenditures are and what purpose they serve. We are supposed to take that on faith.
I started by saying-and I will now repeat in closing-that in accepting this $2 billion proposal we in Canada are putting a burden on the necks of our children and grandchildren. We are acting as if we are not entirely capable of understanding the realities of life.

I should like to express to him, on behalf of hon. members of this House, our congratulations on this auspicious day and wish him many, many years of happiness and health in this place.
The hon. member for Greenwood made some very pertinent points about the defence of the nation. I have every respect for the hon. member but I must take issue with his comments about so-called senseless expenditures on defence. I think that concern has been exhibited by members of the New Democratic Party time and time again. The hon. member talked about the lack of restraint in capital expenditures proposed for the Canadian defence forces. I would point out that it was the restraint in the past that was imposed on capital expenditures for defence forces that brought us to the state we are in today where we must invest in capital works in order to bring our forces to the point where they are capable of maintaining their role in the defence of our nation.
This makes me think of the years between 1918 and 1939 when the United Kingdom found itself in a poor economic condition and had to suffer restraint and cutback. The history of the Royal Air Force shows that it almost ceased to exist because at that time there were some in the country who thought it could be done without. It was only through the efforts of a strong Conservative member between 1935 and 1939 that the Royal Air Force was able to maintain its place in the British military picture. It was Winston Churchill who assured the future of the Royal Air Force for Great Britain. As we know, it turned out to be the saviour of that country in the second world war.
The hon. member for Greenwood suggested that we do not really need a strong defence capability because our good friends to the south have plenty of aircraft and all the things he says we do not need. I would point out to the hon. member that when people become your protectors they cease to be allies. A country must be able to provide some protection for itself; some of the interest in the country's safety must be shown by Canadians.
It seems to me that as elected representatives we cannot allow our defence forces to deteriorate any further. I certainly endorse the move of the minister in upgrading the fighter capability of the Canadian Armed Forces. I back him in the upgrading of the
March 24, 1977

long-range patrol aircraft. Certainly, as the hon. member for Greenwood said, our friends to the south have the capability to protect us, if that is what we want, but I am not sure that this country wants to be protected by the army of another country.
I believe we also have to look to our commitments in Europe, in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Our commitments there will provide us with our first line of defence should an agreement be broken between ourselves and the Soviet Union or the Warsaw Pact nations. I think we owe it to our partners in that organization to provide the young men and women whom we send to represent us in NATO with the best equipment possible. We can send the best troops. We have the best technological people, but without the equipment we might as well keep them at home-which is what our friends in the New Democratic Party would probably have us do-and forsake our commitments to other countries.
The hon. member for Greenwood also said there is no threat to security in the world today that is not nuclear or a missile force. The build-up of Soviet forces within the NATO bloc nations is at the highest point in its history. Since 1945 they have been spending at least 25 per cent of their gross national product on defence and a build-up of their armed forces.

And, as the hon. member says, their navy. The Kiev has been introduced to the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. This is a new picture that has been painted for the defence forces of the allies, if we may use that expression. It is the first time an aircraft carrier has been put into operation by the Soviet Union. We can call it what we want. A picture of it shows that it is an aircraft carrier, no matter what they call it. It is the first instrusion. We cannot look upon it as a missile; we cannot look on it as anything but a conventional type of warship sent by the Soviets to do conventional warfare.
We cannot look ahead and say everything will be taken care of by missiles and nuclear warheads. This is the type of thinking that would get us into difficulty with the Soviet Union.
We must look at how the Soviet Union and its allies have approached their confrontation with our allies up to this point. We must look at the Cuban crisis, at Korea and other areas in which Canadians have been involved. They have used conventional forces to push as far as they possibly can. It is only when they meet determined resistance at the conventional level that they take the stance that they are not interested in overpowering any nation but are interested only in co-existence. If we, or the United States, or any of the free nations of the world want to take the stance that the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact nations are not to be reckoned with in this particular fashion, then we have another think coming, Mr. Chairman. Elistory will prove that.

It seems to me that the New Democratic Party has put forth the idea that we do not have to defend ourselves; that big brother to the south will protect us. Word came out from a meeting of the military committee that some were saying, "When you think of it, I would much rather be red than dead." Canada put its position. One of our delegates, an hon. member of the other place, put my sentiments and I hope the sentiments of all Canadians on the record at this meeting. At that time, Mr. Chairman, a fantastic man by the name of Dr. Louis-Philippe Roy, who was the editor in chief of L'Action Catholique in Quebec City wrote an editorial that should be meditated on today because the problem has remained unsolved and is the same today. I am not accusing anyone but there are indeed over one million people unemployed out of 23 million in Canada. It is not normal to have so many able-bodied people doing nothing-something must be done. And at that time, Dr. Louis-Phillipe Roy asked the following question: Mystery to be solved? It is a mystery that we have to solve tonight with Bill C-45. How to get the money needed to maintain the administration. A mystery to be solved in 1939. A mystery to be solved in 1977. This is what he said: The years go by and the crisis still exists. subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD-SUGGESTED INSTRUCTIONS TO HOSTESS FOODS ON REFUNDING EXCESS PROFITS
ANTI-INFLATION BOARD-SUGGESTED INSTRUCTIONS TO HOSTESS FOODS ON REFUNDING EXCESS PROFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 17, as reported at page 4064 of Hansard, 1 asked the following question of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald):
[The Chairman.]
March 24, 1977
Recently the Anti-Inflation Board ruled that Hostess Foods had made considerable excess profits on the marketing of their potato chips, all in eastern Canada, and to refund this excess profit to the consumer the company plans to issue 20 cent coupons, price reductions and free goods in certain sizes of packages, but all in British Columbia where they have never been in the market. Will the minister give an undertaking that he will instruct Hostess Foods or the Anti-Inflation Board officials to instruct Hostess Foods to restrict the distribution of this cut rate product to the market where they made the excess profit?
Since I asked that question of the Minister of Finance, I have found out that the situation is even worse than I thought. It has now been confirmed that local processors could easily be driven out of business because of this impending action by Hostess Foods. It appears that the firm has elected to break into new western markets, and it is reported that they have bought four vans and hired driver-salesmen to peddle Hostess products around Vancouver and offer the items I have already mentioned. None of this apparently is being passed on to that section of the public that was originally overcharged.
In addition to that, apparently the ruling of the Anti-Inflation Board was made recently and it is now reported that this excess profit was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1.3 million. That is not chicken feed, Mr. Speaker. All of this profit was made in eastern Canada-Ontario, Quebec, and possibly the maritimes. It has since come to my attention that General Foods may be in violation of section 31(1 )(3) of the Combines Investigation Act because they are allegedly planning to engage in the practice of selling a product at a price which is unreasonably low, which will have the effect of substantially eliminating competitors, or which is designed to have that effect.
In addition to that, I find that as early as January, two or three months ago, the management of General Foods was in Las Vegas and there met with the management of some of the local processors and are alleged to have threatened to move in and put them out of business.
There are several issues here. First of all, there is the problem with the Combines Investigation Act and the fact that Hostess Foods could well be in violation of that act. I charge the minister to investigate that and to do it quickly and thoroughly.
Second, it would appear that the company is trying to break into a market by having its excess profits act as a subsidy in breaking into that new market. It seems to me that that is entirely in contravention of the spirit of AIB. Surely the Anti-Inflation Board regulations and legislation were not designed to help a company move into a new market and find ways of getting around the regulations, thereby defeating the local companies. Under the restraint program and the AIB regulations, the market place is a fragile enough institution and we do not need a subsidy of this kind to break companies that are supposed to be well established, or at least have done their own work to establish their market.
In addition to that, one of the local co-operatives is still liable for 1,400 tons of potatoes contracted to local firms. With that kind of contract still having to be fulfilled and an eastern company coming to the market place, what will happen to the local processors?
March 24, 1977

It is also reported that the company plans to build a factory, some kind of processing plant, in Lethbridge, 800 miles away. Presumably it will do so with the funds it will have to refund as a result of the AIB decision. What will that do to the local farmers who are depending on a market they have established through much blood, sweat and tears over the years? Now we have the unconscionable decision on the part of what is a multinational corporation coming in from the U.S., forming a Canadian company in Canada, and then helping to break the Canadian market. It is incumbent on the Minister of Finance to provide an answer for these people to preserve the competitive society that has made our country what it is today and not allow the regulations of the AIB to frustrate the local market and destroy the competition upon which our system is based.
I call upon the minister to correct that situation and ensure that the officials of his department will investigate Hostess Foods, either through the Combines Investigation Act or through the regulations of the AIB. I might add that AIB officials have already conceded the fact that they have made this ruling on Hostess Foods, and I hope the Minister of Finance will press the officials of AIB to make sure that federal laws are not being violated. I hope he will bring Hostess Foods to task and will preserve the market place in an undisturbed fashion in British Columbia, the way it should be protected by a government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD-SUGGESTED INSTRUCTIONS TO HOSTESS FOODS ON REFUNDING EXCESS PROFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question put by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) which was addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on March 17, we think that the question contains a number of assumptions. On behalf of the minister responsible for the Anti-Inflation Board I should like to clarify the situation as it relates to the obligations of Hostess Foods under the Anti-Inflation Act.
The hon. member stated in his question that the AIB had ruled that Hostess Foods had made excess profits. Under the Anti-Inflation Act regulations, the firm files quarterly reports, and the last report signalled a possibility of excess revenue. According to the guidelines, excess revenue is not identified until the close of the firm's fiscal year. Thus Hostess Foods did not have excess revenue, nor did the Anti-Inflation Board rule that the company had excess revenue. However, the company of its own accord is currently taking action to eliminate the possibility of excess revenue by forms of price reduction both in the east and, more extensively, in the west. Since the firm has not yet had excess revenue, it can take any action in any region it chooses.
Under the rules of the anti-inflation program relating to prices and profits, when a firm is identified as having excess revenue that is beyond the level permitted under the program, it must file what is known as a compliance plan to show how it will divest itself of the excess revenue within the following six months. It is this plan which must be approved by the AntiInflation Board, if the need arises.
Adjournment Debate
Nonetheless, I am sure the hon. member from British Columbia will be pleased to report to his constituents that they are able to buy reasonably priced potato chips.

The minister had this to say in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), and I quote from page 4064 of Hansard for March 17, 1977:
I have to point out to the hon. member that in a law passed by this parliament the Anti-Inflation Board has been given the responsibility of making this kind of judgment and, indeed, making appropriate arrangements with the particular firm found in an excess revenue position as to how this is to be returned to the public. In that sense, his suggestion that I might direct the board to do this is counselling an illegality.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED LOAN TO CHILE BY CANADIAN BANKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED LOAN TO CHILE BY CANADIAN BANKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 18, 1976, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) the following question:
-is the Canadian government prepared to convey to the banks Canada's position on the Chilean junta's disrespect for human and civil rights in that unfortunate country and ask them to respect both the moral position of the Canadian government and the technical and economic unacceptability of the loan?
The government well knows the atrocities and abuse of human dignity perpetrated by the vicious Pinochet regime in Chile. It knows full well because Canada voted condemnation of the junta's tactics at the United Nations based on reports by United Nations agencies.
Indeed in its first three years of rule, according to estimates of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, the military dictatorship has killed 30,000 people and imprisoned another 100,000, many of whom were horribly tortured. Hundreds of thousands were expelled from the country, or have themselves sought exile. The junta has suspended congress, outlawed the activities of all political parties, closed down the central workers' federations, many unions and community organizations, censored education, and stifled public freedom of expression, including the press.
Condemnations of the regime have been issued by such international organizations as the United Nations, Amnesty International, the International Labour Organization, and the World Council of Churches.
Pinochet is adamant. He insists that he will never return the country to democratic rule. He is quoted as having said, "I am going to die and the person who succeeds me will also die, but there will be no elections."
Here at home national organizations have expressed their opposition to Canadian participation in helping to bail out the facist regime in power in Chile. For example, the Canadian Labour Congress passed a resolution at its annual convention in May, 1976, which stated that "any corporate investment in Chile at this time oppresses the Chilean people and disgusts their Canadian friends."

March 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Policy statements have been formally adopted by the Anglican and United churches of Canada urging a halt to all investments and loans to Chile until fundamental human rights are restored. Similar positions were expressed by the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops and by the Lutheran church in Canada. Not content with issuing statements, the churches have taken their protests to annual meetings of corporations involved, but were disregarded despite well documented information of human rights violations in Chile.
In spite of this, Mr. Speaker, three Canadian banks-the Royal Bank and the Bank of Nova Scotia are each putting up $8.2 million, and the Toronto-Dominion Bank is putting up $4.2 million-formed part of a United States led consortium to lend $125 million so that the Chilean junta could roll over its debts to European creditors who have been critical of it and unwilling to extend further financing due to human rights violations.
These same banks at home cannot find the money to lend to low-income borrowers because the banks say they are poor risks, but they can find it to lend to the poorest risk in the western hemisphere, the Chilean junta.
In the last days of the Allende government, unemployment stood at a record low of 3 per cent. It has now rocketed to 20 per cent, by official estimates. Outsiders say one out of every four members of the Chilean work force is unemployed; 70 per cent of the workers earn less than $50 per month; a quarter of the population, 2.5 million people, had no income at all by mid-1976 and had to depend on handouts from churches and other humanitarian organizations.
The military has dismantled state involvement in social development and public services. Prices have been allowed to rise astronomically, with inflation running at 340 per cent in 1975 and 174 per cent in 1976, by official figures. The share of national income going to wages and salaries dropped from 63 per cent to 38 per cent in only three years.
The minister's response to me that day was most revealing. He said:
-I would say the banks are already aware of the Canadian government's position with regard to Chile. In so far as exerting any influence, however, this is a private banking transaction and I see no reason why we as a government should interfere in any way.
That argument does not wash, Mr. Speaker. Did the government think it was a private banking transaction when the banks agreed to observe the Arab boycott of companies doing business with Israel? No, the government did not. The government very quickly issued a policy position denouncing the practice. Yet with respect to Chile, where human dignity is involved, they cast a blind eye. I dare say if these were the days of fascist Germany the minister would be saying the same thing. Have we learned nothing from Hitler? Obviously the banks are prepared to do business with Satan himself as long as there is a buck to be made.
I call on the government to put its muscle where its mouth is with respect to moral responsibility for Canadian investment abroad. 1 ask it to declare unequivocally that it disapproves of any Canadian investment in Chile, that its agencies will

finance none, and that it discourages any Canadian investment in Chile until human and civil liberties are restored. Anything less is breaking faith with the thousands of murdered Chileans whose only crime was to exercise the rights of their constitution to belong to a political party and trade union of their choice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs);
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when he put his question on November 18, 1976, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) also had a supplementary for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), asking whether the latter intended to bring forward a legislation to control the export of capital from Canada. The answer was that:
-such legislation in effect would impose exchange control and would not be in the best interest of the Canadian economy.
And the Minister of Finance went on to say:
*-I have no such proposal to put forward.
The question was put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and dealt with loans to Chile by Canadian banks.

It is not the policy of the government to interfere in transactions by Canadian firms or individuals abroad except in compliance with U.N. Security Council decisions. In the instance of the Canadian banks' loan to Chile, I am informed this was a rescheduling of existing debts in which banks from both Canada and the United States participated. The purpose of the loan was to facilitate the eventual repayment of Chilean debts. This was a private loan and there was no basis for Canadian government involvement.
As for our position on human rights violations, the government has made its concern very plain in a variety of international forums and we plan the continue to speak out on these matters.
The minister added, and I quote:
-the banks are already aware of the Canadian government's position with regard to Chile. In so far as exerting an influence, however, this is a private banking transaction and I see no reason why we as a government should interfere in any way.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-COMMISSION OF INQUIRY INTO PROBLEMS IN NEWFOUNDLAND-TERMS OF REFERENCE AND DATE OF COMMENCEMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-COMMISSION OF INQUIRY INTO PROBLEMS IN NEWFOUNDLAND-TERMS OF REFERENCE AND DATE OF COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) what action he was taking in connection with a royal commission to investigate modes of transportation into, from, and across Newfoundland, he replied that I could expect an answer on the appointment perhaps within one week. This royal commission was suggested on December 1, 1976, by Mr. Bandeen of the CNR.
March 24, 1977

This suggestion was accepted by the Newfoundland government and the railway union, so long as, first, CN maintained the present level of services and employment while the investigation was under way, and second, so long as federal obligations with respect to transportation matters generally, such as further assistance for repairs and extensions of the trans-Canada highway, DREE roads and the like were continued.
The minister said he was going to appoint this commission. Mr. Bandeen said that it should not take it longer than six months to do its work. The minister said it should report this year's, 1977. Well, 112 days later the royal commission is still not appointed. Why the delay, Mr. Speaker? The minister does not delay when he goes travelling; he goes pretty quickly. Why did he delay 112 days in appointing the royal commission which is urgently needed.
I know that Dr. Arthur Sullivan of Memorial University, St. John's, is supposed to be the chairman. This has been widely known for between four and six weeks. I know that Mr. Esau Thomas of Placentia, the railway union leader, is to be one of the members. I know those hon. gentlemen are looking for a third member to represent the user or business community. Surely we do not have to wait 112 days to find members of a royal commission on such an important matter as this. Surely other Newfoundlanders must be willing to serve, although perhaps an appointment to a Liberal royal commission now is not too desirable.
Since this suggestion was made by Dr. Bandeen and accepted, the Minister of Transport has abandoned the user-pay concept. He has beaten a hasty retreat from the user-pay; of course he was headed off in that direction by his colleagues who informed him that he would be grounded unless he abandoned the user-pay concept.
There are important transportation problems in Newfoundland which must be solved. Just last summer the minister snatched the buses from the control of the board of commissioners of public utilities of Newfoundland, and put them under the Canadian Transport Commission. We learned a few days ago why he did that when the Canadian Transport Commission brought down a decision allowing the CN buses to charge another 8 per cent increase in Newfoundland, in addition to the 30 per cent increase they had taken in June, in defiance of the public utilities commission of Newfoundland.
The Canadian Transport Commission, in my opinion, should have a sign over its door reading, "Abandon hope all ye who oppose rate increases and appear here." The hearing is only a formality. The Canadian Transport Commission has neither the time nor the interest to be concerned about bus transportation and the general transport situation in Newfoundland. That should be regulated at the local level. The hearing before the CTC was unsatisfactory and perfunctory. Adjournments were not allowed to interested parties. The rates have increased 8 per cent, and we hear promises that there will be further applications for more increases.
We have many problems. The trans-Canada highway on which most of our freight now moves into and out of Newfoundland is deteriorating before our very eyes. The minister
Adjournment Debate
of highways of Newfoundland says that he hopes the government of Canada is going to provide financial assistance to improve and upgrade that highway. I hope he is not being over-optimistic. I see no sign of his hopes being fulfilled, although there may be some chance if an election is to take place in the next six months or one year. That problem is very serious.
What is to happen with regard to the losses of the CN in Newfoundland? I say the main problem is that the Government of Canada is not accepting its financial obligations. I do not blame the CN. It is losing S23 million a year. If that railway service must operate at a loss, the Government of Canada is under the constitutional and legal obligation to meet that loss. If the CN drydock, for which the government has an obligation, operates at a loss, I say that the government is under an obligation to overcome that situation. The Government of Canada should help it meet its losses and expand its facilities. I hope to go into greater detail on this topic in another debate. That is another transportation associated problem in Newfoundland.
This royal commission will have to look at the shipping service in Newfoundland. I just received notification that the Clarke Transportation Service, which operates a shipping service from Montreal to St. John's and Corner Brook, and is subsidized by the Government of Canada, recently increased its rates for pool car shipments by 10 per cent, its highest increase for any Canadian service, from Montreal to Newfoundland. Has the Canadian government agreed to this increase? If the Canadian government subsidizes the service, it must surely have the right to say what increases are going to occur.
There are many, many problems of transportation service in Newfoundland that require action, not further study. However, if there is to be further study, every day counts before the chaos in the transportation system in Newfoundland causes complete collapse.
I received a letter from a railway employee a few days ago. There are some 3,500 people who still work for CN in Newfoundland. These people are very concerned. They see the service deteriorating before their eyes. This gentleman told me that in Clarenville alone there are five diesel locomotive engines lying idle, and that train service to Bonavista is down to one a week. The railway will not accept freight unless it is in pool car loads. Any freight that will not fill a pool car is sent by its truck service. CN has its own truck service. It competes with its own rail service by using its own trucks. The service is losing money. It is mostly subsidized.
I call on the minister to meet his obligations when he is in Newfoundland next week, appoint this royal commission, get on with this job, get this report, and take some action to help Newfoundland in its transportation needs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-COMMISSION OF INQUIRY INTO PROBLEMS IN NEWFOUNDLAND-TERMS OF REFERENCE AND DATE OF COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member directed a question to the minister on March 22. I quote the minister's reply at that time. He said:
4330

March 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, we have been discussing these questions with the government of Newfoundland and others. We are now nearly at the stage of having the matter in final form and I would expect an announcement within perhaps one week.
Discussions have been ongoing between Transport Canada and the government of Newfoundland concerning a commission of inquiry to investigate all aspects of transportation for Newfoundland, and have resulted in agreement that such a commission is appropriate.
It is intended that a commission would be guided in its endeavours by terms of reference sufficiently broad in scope that transportation related questions can be examined with a perspective capable of recognizing social and economic objectives of the two governments. A commission would be asked to articulate clearly the real wishes and needs of Newfoundland, based on contributions received from all interested parties through the public hearing process. It will carefully weigh all factors in arriving at a clear statement of priorities and plans for improving the transportation system.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker I would like to say the minister hopes to be in a position within the next week to make a detailed announcement on the commission.
